content: Polio is a severe and potentially life-threatening disease caused by a virus that primarily targets the nervous system. It is most commonly transmitted from person to person through contact with stool (feces) of an infected individual. Less commonly, it can spread via respiratory droplets from a sneeze or cough of an infected person. You can contract polio in the following ways: Consuming raw or undercooked food, or drinking water or other beverages contaminated with the stool of an infected person. Putting contaminated objects, such as toys, into your mouth. Touching contaminated objects and then placing your fingers in your mouth. Having close contact with someone who is ill with polio, such as while caring for them. Most individuals infected with polio do not exhibit symptoms. Some may experience mild symptoms, including fever, fatigue, nausea, headache, nasal congestion, sore throat, cough, stiffness in the neck and back, and pain in the stomach, arms, or legs. The majority of people recover completely. In rare cases, the polio virus can invade the brain and spinal cord, leading to permanent muscle function loss (paralysis), typically in the legs or arms. If the muscles responsible for breathing are affected, or if the brain becomes infected, the disease can result in death. Who is at risk? Polio remains a concern in certain regions of the world. Individuals who are not up to date with their polio vaccinations are at risk of contracting the disease. Even if you are vaccinated, traveling to a country where polio is still present may require a one-time adult booster dose of the polio vaccine. It is essential to check the travel health recommendations for your destination and consult with your healthcare provider to determine if additional vaccinations are necessary before your trip. What can travelers do to prevent polio? Ensure your polio vaccinations are up to date. If you are traveling to a polio-affected country, you may need a one-time adult booster dose of the vaccine. Consult your healthcare provider and review your destination’s travel health page for specific recommendations. Make sure children are vaccinated. For optimal protection, children should receive four doses of the polio vaccine at the following ages: 2 months 4 months 6 through 18 months A booster dose at 4 through 6 years of age. Choose safer food and drinks while traveling Follow food and drink safety guidelines to avoid consuming items that may be contaminated with the stool of a person infected with polio. This includes avoiding raw or undercooked food and ensuring that water and beverages are safe to drink. Wash your hands frequently Wash your hands thoroughly with soap and water, especially after using the bathroom, changing a child’s diaper, and before eating or preparing food. Note that alcohol-based hand sanitizers are not effective against the poliovirus. Avoid touching your eyes, nose, or mouth. If you must touch your face, ensure your hands are clean. When coughing or sneezing, cover your mouth and nose with a tissue or your sleeve (not your hands) to prevent the spread of germs.
